question.html:
An ideal gas undergoes four different processes from the same initial state as shown in the figure below. Those processes are adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric. The curve which represents the adiabatic process among 1, 2, 3 and 4 is

question.stem: An ideal gas undergoes four different processes from the same initial state as shown in the figure below. Those processes are adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric. The curve which represents the adiabatic process among 1, 2, 3 and 4 is

figures.text: P-V diagram: four processes 1, 2, 3, 4 from the same initial state

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: P-V diagram: four processes 1, 2, 3, 4 from the same initial state

solution.full_text:
1. $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adiabatic}} = -\gamma P$
2. $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{isothermal}} = -P$
3. $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adiabatic}} > \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{isothermal}}$
[Figure: P-V diagram of isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric processes from one initial state]
solution.html:
1. (dPdV)adiabatic = -γ P
  2. (dPdV)isothermal = -P
  3. (dPdV)adiabatic > (dPdV)isothermal
steps: $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adiabatic}} = -\gamma P$
$\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{isothermal}} = -P$
$\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adiabatic}} > \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{isothermal}}$

figures.text: P-V diagram of isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric processes from one initial state

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: P-V diagram of isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric processes from one initial state

steps: Curve $1$ is vertical ($V$ constant), so it is isochoric.
Curve $4$ is horizontal ($P$ constant), so it is isobaric.
For the isothermal process $PV = \text{const}$, so $\frac{dP}{dV} = -\frac{P}{V}$.
For the adiabatic process $PV^{\gamma} = \text{const}$, so $\frac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma\frac{P}{V}$.
Since $\gamma > 1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
Curve $2$ is steeper than curve $3$, so curve $2$ is adiabatic, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Curve 1 is vertical (V constant), so it is isochoric.
  2. Curve 4 is horizontal (P constant), so it is isobaric.
  3. For the isothermal process PV = const, so dPdV = -PV.
  4. For the adiabatic process PVγ = const, so dPdV = -γPV.
  5. Since γ > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
  6. Curve 2 is steeper than curve 3, so curve 2 is adiabatic, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Curve 1 is vertical (isochoric), 4 horizontal (isobaric); of the two falling curves the steeper one (2) is adiabatic since its slope is gamma times the isothermal slope.

chapter.name: Thermodynamics
chapter.why: The answer turns on identifying the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram by comparing slopes of adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric processes, which is thermodynamics.

subtopics.name: Adiabatic Process
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram being steeper than the isothermal curve (slope -gamma P/V versus -P/V), a property of the adiabatic process.

step_list: Eliminate the straight lines: the vertical line (constant V) is isochoric and the horizontal line (constant P) is isobaric, leaving the two curves
Recall that the adiabatic slope dP/dV = -gamma P/V is gamma times the isothermal slope -P/V, so the adiabatic is the steeper of the two curves from the common initial point and pick that curve
difficulty.why: The work is identifying the isochoric and isobaric lines by sight, then using the gamma-times-steeper slope relation to tell the adiabatic curve from the isothermal one.

source.note: Stem figure is a P-V graph with curves labelled 1-4. Text-layer draft had a stray trailing 'dP' fragment (from figure axis label), excluded from stem.

categories.concept: On a $P$-$V$ diagram the adiabatic and the isothermal both fall, and the adiabatic is the steeper of the two because its slope carries the extra factor $\gamma$

An adiabatic change is the gentler of the two, so it is curve 3.
steps.fix: At the same point the adiabatic slope is $\gamma$ times the isothermal slope and $\gamma > 1$, so the adiabatic falls faster -- the steeper curve, 2.

question.full_text:
The angular speed of a fly wheel moving with uniform angular acceleration changes from $1200\,\mathrm{rpm}$ to $3120\,\mathrm{rpm}$ in $16$ seconds. The angular acceleration in $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$ is
(1) $2\pi$
(2) $4\pi$
(3) $12\pi$
(4) $104\pi$
question.html:
The angular speed of a fly wheel moving with uniform angular acceleration changes from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 seconds. The angular acceleration in rad/s2 is
  1. (1)2π
  2. (2)4π
  3. (3)12π
  4. (4)104π
question.stem: The angular speed of a fly wheel moving with uniform angular acceleration changes from $1200\,\mathrm{rpm}$ to $3120\,\mathrm{rpm}$ in $16$ seconds. The angular acceleration in $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Angular acceleration $\alpha = \frac{\omega_f - \omega_i}{t}$
2. $\omega_f = 3120 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
3. $\omega_i = 1200 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
4. $\Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{(3120 - 1200)}{16} \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 4\pi$
solution.html:
1. Angular acceleration α = ωf - ωit
  2. ωf = 3120 × 2π60 rad/s
  3. ωi = 1200 × 2π60 rad/s
  4. ⇒ α = (3120 - 1200)16 × 2π60 = 4π
steps: Angular acceleration $\alpha = \frac{\omega_f - \omega_i}{t}$
$\omega_f = 3120 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
$\omega_i = 1200 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
$\Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{(3120 - 1200)}{16} \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 4\pi$
Change in angular speed: $\Delta n = 3120 - 1200 = 1920\,\mathrm{rpm}$.
Convert to rev/s: $\frac{1920}{60} = 32\,\mathrm{rev/s}$.
Convert to rad/s: $\Delta\omega = 2\pi \times 32 = 64\pi\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{t} = \frac{64\pi}{16} = 4\pi\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Change in angular speed: Δ n = 3120 - 1200 = 1920 rpm.
  2. Convert to rev/s: 192060 = 32 rev/s.
  3. Convert to rad/s: Δω = 2π × 32 = 64π rad/s.
  4. α = Δωt = 64π16 = 4π rad/s2, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Change in speed 1920 rpm = 32 rev/s = 64π rad/s over 16 s gives α = 4π rad/s^2.

question.stem: In the given circuits (a), (b) and (c), the potential drop across the two $p$-$n$ junctions are equal in

figures.text: Three circuits (a), (b), (c): two p-n junctions joined in series across a cell

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Three circuits (a), (b), (c): two p-n junctions joined in series across a cell

solution.full_text:
1. Potential drops across the $p$-$n$ junctions will be same if either both junctions are forward biased or both junction are reverse biased.
2. In figure (a) and (c), both junctions are forward biased therefore both have same potential.
3. In figure (b) first junction is forward biased and second junction is reverse biased, so both junctions have different potential difference.

  2. In figure (a) and (c), both junctions are forward biased therefore both have same potential.
  3. In figure (b) first junction is forward biased and second junction is reverse biased, so both junctions have different potential difference.

In figure (b) first junction is forward biased and second junction is reverse biased, so both junctions have

steps: In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented $P\to N$ in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give $V_1 = V_2$.
In circuit (b) one junction is $P\to N$ and the other $N\to P$, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; $V_{\text{forward}} \ll V_{\text{reverse}}$, so the drops are unequal.
In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented $N\to P$ in series, so both have the same bias and $V_1 = V_2$.
Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented P→ N in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give V1 = V2.
  2. In circuit (b) one junction is P→ N and the other N→ P, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; Vforward ≪ Vreverse, so the drops are unequal.
  3. In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented N→ P in series, so both have the same bias and V1 = V2.
  4. Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: In (a) and (c) both junctions face the same way in series, so both are equally forward (or reverse) biased and the drops are equal; in (b) one is forward and one reverse biased, so the drops differ.

chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics
chapter.why: The answer turns on the forward/reverse bias behaviour of p-n junction diodes in each circuit, which is semiconductor electronics.

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopics.why: The answer depends on recognising that the two series diodes are both identically biased in circuits (a) and (c) but one forward- and one reverse-biased in circuit (b), so the drops are equal only when both share the same bias state.

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
subtopics.why: Circuit (b) joins a PN and an NP junction in series, so one is reverse-biased and takes almost the whole drop, and ruling (b) out depends on that reverse-bias behaviour.

step_list: Read each circuit to find the orientation of the two series p-n junctions relative to the cell, deciding whether each is forward or reverse biased
Recognise that when both junctions in series have the same bias (both forward or both reverse) and are identical, the same current flows through them and the voltage divides equally
Recognise that when one is forward and the other reverse biased, the reverse-biased junction takes nearly all the voltage, so the drops are unequal, and pick the circuits with matching orientations
difficulty.why: The work is a bias reading of six junctions across three circuits followed by applying series-current reasoning to decide when the two drops are equal, including the case where both are reverse biased.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Single-circuit options (a) only and (c) only are the result of assuming drops are equal only when both junctions conduct, overlooking that two identical reverse-biased junctions also share the voltage equally.

source.note: Figure above the stem shows three circuits (a), (b), (c), each with two p-n junction blocks and a cell; figure_bbox covers all three. p-n printed in italics in the source.

categories.concept: Two junctions in series facing the same way carry the same current and share the applied voltage equally; a back-to-back pair puts one in forward and one in reverse bias, and almost all the voltage falls across the reverse-biased one

trap.label: half_right
trap.route: Circuit (a) is read correctly as two junctions pointing the same way, and circuit (c) is then set aside because its blocks are printed N before P, the opposite way round from (a), so a true answer is given with one of its two members missing.
trap.who: a student who tests the first circuit, finds the two junctions alike, and reads the order the letters are printed in as the orientation that matters
trap.feels: everything the option claims is true, and (c) does look different from (a) on the page because the P and N blocks are printed in the other order

steps.text: In (a) both junctions run P to N in the same sense, so the same current passes and the drops are equal.
In (c) the blocks read N then P, the other way round, so (c) is a different case and the answer is (a) only.
steps.fix: What matters is whether the two junctions in one circuit face the same way as each other, not which letter is drawn first; in (c) both are N then P, so they match each other and share the voltage equally too.

other_options.who: a student who reads equal sharing as a matter of the arrangement looking symmetric
other_options.feels: circuit (b) is the one drawn as a mirror pair, with the two junctions facing each other, and a symmetric arrangement looks like one that must divide the voltage evenly

steps.text: The two junctions in (b) are oppositely oriented, so the circuit is symmetric about its middle.
A symmetric pair must share the applied voltage equally, so (b) is the circuit.
steps.fix: Oppositely oriented junctions in series mean one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; the reverse-biased one passes almost no current and nearly the whole emf appears across it.

other_options.proof: compared the two circuits this option separates: (a) and (c) are identical in the only feature the question turns on -- two junctions in series oriented the same way as each other, so one current and one shared voltage -- and differ only in whether that pair is drawn P-N or N-P; any reading that accepts (c) accepts (a) as well, so no route stops at (c) alone

A shell of mass $m$ is at rest initially. It explodes into three fragments having mass in the ratio $2:2:1$. If the fragments having equal mass fly off along mutually perpendicular directions with speed $v$, the speed of the third (lighter) fragment is

(2) $\sqrt{2}v$
(3) $2\sqrt{2}v$
(4) $3\sqrt{2}v$

  2. (2)2v
  3. (3)22v
  4. (4)32v
question.stem: A shell of mass $m$ is at rest initially. It explodes into three fragments having mass in the ratio $2:2:1$. If the fragments having equal mass fly off along mutually perpendicular directions with speed $v$, the speed of the third (lighter) fragment is

solution.full_text:
1. Momentum of the system would remain conserved.
2. Initial momentum $= 0$
3. Final momentum should also be zero.
4. Let masses be $2m$, $2m$, and $m$
5. Momentum along $x$-direction $= 2mv\hat{i}$
6. Momentum along $y$-direction $= 2mv\hat{j}$
7. Net momentum $= \sqrt{(2mv)^{2} + (2mv)^{2}} = \sqrt{2} \cdot 2mv$
8. Now, $2\sqrt{2}mv = mv'$
9. $v' = 2\sqrt{2}v$

2. It is analogous to Coulomb's law, where $Id\vec{l}$ is vector source and electric field is produced by scalar source $q$.
3. Here statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect.

steps.text: Statement I is right: Biot-Savart's law gives $dB$ for a current element $Idl$.

question.full_text:
The ratio of the radius of gyration of a thin uniform disc about an axis passing through its centre and normal to its plane to the radius of gyration of the disc about its diameter is
(1) $2:1$
(2) $\sqrt{2}:1$
(3) $4:1$
(4) $1:\sqrt{2}$
question.html:
The ratio of the radius of gyration of a thin uniform disc about an axis passing through its centre and normal to its plane to the radius of gyration of the disc about its diameter is
  1. (1)2:1
  2. (2)2:1
  3. (3)4:1
  4. (4)1:2
question.stem: The ratio of the radius of gyration of a thin uniform disc about an axis passing through its centre and normal to its plane to the radius of gyration of the disc about its diameter is

solution.full_text:
[Figure: A disc seen face-on with its axis normal to the plane (into the page) and a curved arrow showing rotation about it]
1. $I_1 = \frac{MR^2}{2}$
2. $k_1 = \sqrt{\frac{I_1}{M}}$
3. $= \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$
[Figure: A disc seen edge-on as a circle, with a vertical axis along its diameter and a curved rotation arrow at the top]
4. $I_2 = \frac{MR^2}{4}$
5. $k_2 = \sqrt{\frac{I_2}{M}}$
6. $= \frac{R}{2}$
7. $\frac{k_1}{k_2} = \frac{\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{R}{2}}$
8. $= \sqrt{2} : 1$

1. I1 = MR22
  2. k1 = I1M
  3. = R2
  4. I2 = MR24
  5. k2 = I2M
  6. = R2
  7. k1k2 = R2R2
  8. = 2 : 1

$= \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$
$k_2 = \sqrt{\frac{I_2}{M}}$
$\frac{k_1}{k_2} = \frac{\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{R}{2}}$

steps: For a thin uniform disc about the axis through the centre normal to its plane, $I_1 = \frac{MR^2}{2}$, so $k_1 = \sqrt{\frac{I_1}{M}} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.
By the perpendicular axis theorem, $I_1 = 2I_d$, so $I_d = \frac{MR^2}{4}$.
Hence $k_2 = \sqrt{\frac{I_d}{M}} = \frac{R}{2}$.
$\frac{k_1}{k_2} = \frac{R/\sqrt{2}}{R/2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$, so the ratio is $\sqrt{2}:1$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For a thin uniform disc about the axis through the centre normal to its plane, I1 = MR22, so k1 = I1M = R2.
  2. By the perpendicular axis theorem, I1 = 2Id, so Id = MR24.
  3. Hence k2 = IdM = R2.
  4. k1k2 = R/2R/2 = 22 = 2, so the ratio is 2:1, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: k_normal = R/sqrt2 (I = MR^2/2), k_diameter = R/2 (I = MR^2/4), so ratio = sqrt2 : 1.

steps.text: $I$ about the normal axis is $\frac{MR^2}{2}$ and about a diameter is $\frac{MR^2}{4}$.
Their ratio is $2:1$.
So the radii of gyration are in the ratio $2:1$.
steps.fix: $k=\sqrt{I/M}$: take the square root of the $I$ ratio, giving $\sqrt{2}:1$.

other_options.who: a student who does the whole calculation correctly but divides the diameter axis by the normal axis
other_options.feels: $1:\sqrt{2}$ carries the same $\sqrt{2}$ the working produced, so the answer looks already found

steps.text: $k_{\perp} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $k_{d} = \frac{R}{2}$.
Form $\frac{k_d}{k_{\perp}} = \frac{R/2}{R/\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
steps.fix: The stem names the normal-axis radius of gyration first, so it belongs in the numerator: $\sqrt{2}:1$.

other_options.proof: Listed the single-step routes: radii of gyration give $\sqrt{2}:1$, the moments of inertia give $2:1$, and taking either the wrong way round gives $1:\sqrt{2}$ or $1:2$ — the first three are printed. $4:1$ is the $I$ ratio squared, so reaching it needs the ratio of moments of inertia taken and then squared instead of rooted, two opposite errors in one line.

solution.full_text:
1. We know,
2. RMS value of A.C. $E_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
3. $E_0 = \sqrt{2}E_{\mathrm{rms}}$

  2. RMS value of A.C. Erms = E02

steps: We know,
RMS value of A.C. $E_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
$E_0 = \sqrt{2}E_{\mathrm{rms}}$
For a sinusoidal source, $V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $V_0 = \sqrt{2}\,V_{rms}$, which is option $3$.

question.full_text:
The energy that will be ideally radiated by a $100\,\mathrm{kW}$ transmitter in $1\,\mathrm{hour}$ is
(1) $36 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$
(2) $36 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{J}$
(3) $36 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$
(4) $1 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$
question.html:
The energy that will be ideally radiated by a 100 kW transmitter in 1 hour is
  1. (1)36 × 107 J
  2. (2)36 × 104 J
  3. (3)36 × 105 J
  4. (4)1 × 105 J
question.stem: The energy that will be ideally radiated by a $100\,\mathrm{kW}$ transmitter in $1\,\mathrm{hour}$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Energy $=$ Power $\times$ time
2. $E = 100 \times 10^{3} \times 3600$
3. $= 36 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$
solution.html:
1. Energy = Power × time
  2. E = 100 × 103 × 3600
  3. = 36 × 107 J
steps: Energy $=$ Power $\times$ time
$= 36 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$
Energy radiated $E = P\,t$.
$P = 100\,\mathrm{kW} = 10^{5}\,\mathrm{W}$ and $t = 1\,\mathrm{h} = 3600\,\mathrm{s}$.
$E = 10^{5} \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{J} = 36 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Energy radiated E = P t.
  2. P = 100 kW = 105 W and t = 1 h = 3600 s.
  3. E = 105 × 3600 = 3.6 × 108 J = 36 × 107 J, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Energy = power x time = 100000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^8 J = 36 x 10^7 J.

question.full_text:
In a Young’s double slit experiment, a student observes 8 fringes in a certain segment of screen when a monochromatic light of $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ wavelength is used. If the wavelength of light is changed to $400\,\mathrm{nm}$, then the number of fringes he would observe in the same region of the screen is
(1) 6
(2) 8
(3) 9
(4) 12
question.html:
In a Young’s double slit experiment, a student observes 8 fringes in a certain segment of screen when a monochromatic light of 600 nm wavelength is used. If the wavelength of light is changed to 400 nm, then the number of fringes he would observe in the same region of the screen is
  1. (1)6
  2. (2)8
  3. (3)9
  4. (4)12
question.stem: In a Young’s double slit experiment, a student observes 8 fringes in a certain segment of screen when a monochromatic light of $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ wavelength is used. If the wavelength of light is changed to $400\,\mathrm{nm}$, then the number of fringes he would observe in the same region of the screen is

solution.full_text:
1. $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$
2. Let length of segment of screen $= l$
3. $\Rightarrow l = 8\beta_1 = \frac{8\lambda_1 D}{d}$ ...(1)
4. and $l = n\beta_2 = \frac{n\lambda_2 D}{d}$ ...(2)
5. from (1) and (2)
6. $8\lambda_1 = n\lambda_2$
7. $8(600\,\mathrm{nm}) = n(400\,\mathrm{nm})$
8. $n = 12$
solution.html:
1. β = λ Dd
  2. Let length of segment of screen = l
  3. ⇒ l = 8β1 = 8λ1 Dd ...(1)
  4. and l = nβ2 = nλ2 Dd ...(2)
  5. from (1) and (2)
  6. 8λ1 = nλ2
  7. 8(600 nm) = n(400 nm)
  8. n = 12
steps: $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$
Let length of segment of screen $= l$
$\Rightarrow l = 8\beta_1 = \frac{8\lambda_1 D}{d}$ ...(1)
and $l = n\beta_2 = \frac{n\lambda_2 D}{d}$ ...(2)
from (1) and (2)
$8\lambda_1 = n\lambda_2$
$8(600\,\mathrm{nm}) = n(400\,\mathrm{nm})$
printed_lines: Let length of segment of screen = l

steps: Fringe width $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$, so $\beta \propto \lambda$.
For the same segment of length $L$, $L = n_1\beta_1 = n_2\beta_2$, so $n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2$.
$n_2 = \frac{8 \times 600\,\mathrm{nm}}{400\,\mathrm{nm}} = 12$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Fringe width β = λ Dd, so β ∝ λ.
  2. For the same segment of length L, L = n1β1 = n2β2, so n1λ1 = n2λ2.
  3. n2 = 8 × 600 nm400 nm = 12, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Fringe width is proportional to wavelength, so n*lambda is constant for a fixed region: 8 x 600 = n x 400 gives n = 12.

chapter.name: Wave Optics
chapter.why: The answer turns on YDSE fringe width being proportional to wavelength, so the same region holds 8 x 600/400 = 12 fringes, which is wave optics.

subtopics.name: Fringe Width in YDSE
subtopics.why: The answer depends on fringe width being proportional to wavelength (beta = lambda D / d), so n1 lambda1 = n2 lambda2 gives 8 x 600 = n x 400, n = 12.

step_list: Recall that fringe width beta = lambda*D/d, so for a fixed segment of screen the number of fringes times the fringe width is constant, i.e. n1*lambda1 = n2*lambda2
Substitute n1 = 8, lambda1 = 600 nm, lambda2 = 400 nm and solve for n2
difficulty.why: The work is one recall (fringe width proportional to wavelength) turned into an inverse proportion between fringe count and wavelength, followed by a single ratio calculation.

source.note: Text-layer draft had stray trailing characters 'λ D' after the stem; these are not present in the image and were excluded.

categories.concept: Fringe width is proportional to wavelength, so in a fixed stretch of screen the number of fringes varies inversely with wavelength

trap.label: reversed
trap.route: The fringe count is read as proportional to the wavelength rather than inversely, so cutting 600 nm to 400 nm is taken to cut the count: $8\times\frac{400}{600}\approx5.3$, and 6 is the only option below 8.
trap.who: a student who remembers $\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$ as 'smaller wavelength, smaller pattern' and transfers that straight to the number of fringes
trap.feels: shorter wavelength does shrink everything about the pattern, so fewer fringes sounds like the same statement

steps.text: Fringe width $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$ falls when the wavelength falls.

question.stem: Two resistors of resistance, $100\,\Omega$ and $200\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel in an electrical circuit. The ratio of the thermal energy developed in $100\,\Omega$ to that in $200\,\Omega$ in a given time is

1. For parallel combination
2. $P = \frac{V^2}{R}$
3. $\frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{R_2}{R_1}$
4. $\Rightarrow \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{200}{100} = \frac{2}{1}$

  3. P1P2 = R2R1

steps: For parallel combination
$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{200}{100} = \frac{2}{1}$
In a parallel connection both resistors have the same potential difference $V$.
Heat developed in time $t$ is $H = \frac{V^2 t}{R}$, so $H \propto \frac{1}{R}$.

question.full_text:
The ratio of the distances travelled by a freely falling body in the $1^{\text{st}}$, $2^{\text{nd}}$, $3^{\text{rd}}$ and $4^{\text{th}}$ second
(1) $1:2:3:4$
(2) $1:4:9:16$
(3) $1:3:5:7$
(4) $1:1:1:1$

The ratio of the distances travelled by a freely falling body in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th second
  1. (1)1:2:3:4
  2. (2)1:4:9:16
  3. (3)1:3:5:7
  4. (4)1:1:1:1
question.stem: The ratio of the distances travelled by a freely falling body in the $1^{\text{st}}$, $2^{\text{nd}}$, $3^{\text{rd}}$ and $4^{\text{th}}$ second

solution.full_text:
1. $S_{n^{\text{th}}} = u + \frac{1}{2}a(2n - 1)$
2. $S_{1^{\text{st}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 1 - 1) = \frac{g}{2}$
3. $S_{2^{\text{nd}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 2 - 1) = 3\left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
4. $S_{3^{\text{rd}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 3 - 1) = 5 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
5. $S_{4^{\text{th}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 4 - 1) = 7 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
6. $S_{1^{\text{st}}} : S_{2^{\text{nd}}} : S_{3^{\text{rd}}} : S_{4^{\text{th}}} = 1 : 3 : 5 : 7$
solution.html:
1. Snth = u + 12a(2n - 1)
  2. S1st = 12g(2 × 1 - 1) = g2
  3. S2nd = 12g(2 × 2 - 1) = 3(12g)
  4. S3rd = 12g(2 × 3 - 1) = 5 × (12g)
  5. S4th = 12g(2 × 4 - 1) = 7 × (12g)
  6. S1st : S2nd : S3rd : S4th = 1 : 3 : 5 : 7
steps: $S_{2^{\text{nd}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 2 - 1) = 3\left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
$S_{3^{\text{rd}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 3 - 1) = 5 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
$S_{4^{\text{th}}} = \frac{1}{2}g(2 \times 4 - 1) = 7 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}g\right)$
For a body starting from rest ($u=0$), distance in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is $s_n = u + \frac{g}{2}(2n-1) = \frac{g}{2}(2n-1)$.
Ratio $s_1:s_2:s_3:s_4 = 1:3:5:7$, which is option $3$.

  2. For n=1,2,3,4: s1=g2, s2=3g2, s3=5g2, s4=7g2.
  3. Ratio s1:s2:s3:s4 = 1:3:5:7, which is option 3.

question.full_text:
When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$, the velocity of light, $v$ is given by ($c$-velocity of light in vacuum)
(1) $v = c$
(2) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_r}{\varepsilon_r}}$
(3) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\varepsilon_r}{\mu_r}}$
(4) $v = \dfrac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
question.html:
When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity εr and relative permeability μr, the velocity of light, v is given by (c-velocity of light in vacuum)
  1. (1)v = c
  2. (2)v = μrεr
  3. (3)v = εrμr
  4. (4)v = cεr μr
question.stem: When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$, the velocity of light, $v$ is given by ($c$-velocity of light in vacuum)

solution.full_text:
1. $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_m \mu_m}}$
2. $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mu_0 \mu_r}}$
3. Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}}$
4. $\Rightarrow v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
solution.html:
1. v = 1εm μm
  2. v = 1ε0 εr μ0 μr
  3. Since c = 1ε0 μ0
  4. ⇒ v = cεr μr
steps: $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_m \mu_m}}$
$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mu_0 \mu_r}}$
Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}}$
$\Rightarrow v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
In a medium, $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu \varepsilon}}$ with $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r$ and $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r$.
$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_r \varepsilon_r}}$.
Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$, $v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In a medium, v = 1μ ε with μ = μ0 μr and ε = ε0 εr.
  2. v = 1μ0 ε0 · 1μr εr.
  3. Since c = 1μ0 ε0, v = cεr μr, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) = 1/sqrt(mu0 mu_r eps0 eps_r) = c/sqrt(eps_r mu_r).

2. Now, $Q$ = same
3. $\Rightarrow V \propto \frac{1}{R} \Rightarrow$ more the radius less will be the potential.
4. $\Rightarrow$ Hence potential would be more on smaller sphere

  2. Now, Q = same

$\Rightarrow$ Hence potential would be more on smaller sphere

steps: For a charged hollow conducting sphere, the potential is $V = \frac{kQ}{R}$.

question.full_text:
A copper wire of length $10\,\mathrm{m}$ and radius $\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\,\mathrm{m}$ has electrical resistance of $10\,\Omega$. The current density in the wire for an electric field strength of $10\,(\mathrm{V/m})$ is
(1) $10^{4}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
(2) $10^{6}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
(3) $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
(4) $10^{5}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
question.html:
A copper wire of length 10 m and radius (10-2π) m has electrical resistance of 10 Ω. The current density in the wire for an electric field strength of 10 (V/m) is
  1. (1)104 A/m2
  2. (2)106 A/m2
  3. (3)10-5 A/m2
  4. (4)105 A/m2
question.stem: A copper wire of length $10\,\mathrm{m}$ and radius $\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\,\mathrm{m}$ has electrical resistance of $10\,\Omega$. The current density in the wire for an electric field strength of $10\,(\mathrm{V/m})$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Resistance, $R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \frac{L}{\sigma A}$
2. $\Rightarrow \sigma = \frac{L}{RA}$
3. Also current density $j = \sigma E = \frac{LE}{RA}$
4. $j = \frac{10 \times 10}{10 \times \pi\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}} = \frac{100}{10 \times \pi \times \left(\frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}\right)}$
5. $= 10^{5}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
solution.html:
1. Resistance, R = ρLA = Lσ A
  2. ⇒ σ = LRA
  3. Also current density j = σ E = LERA
  4. j = 10 × 1010 × π(10-2π)2 = 10010 × π × (10-4π)
  5. = 105 A/m2
steps: Resistance, $R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \frac{L}{\sigma A}$
$\Rightarrow \sigma = \frac{L}{RA}$
Also current density $j = \sigma E = \frac{LE}{RA}$
$j = \frac{10 \times 10}{10 \times \pi\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}} = \frac{100}{10 \times \pi \times \left(\frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}\right)}$
Cross-sectional area: $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
Resistivity: $\rho = \frac{RA}{l} = \frac{10 \times 10^{-4}}{10} = 10^{-4}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$.
Current density: $J = \sigma E = \frac{E}{\rho} = \frac{10}{10^{-4}} = 10^{5}\,\mathrm{A/m^2}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Cross-sectional area: A = π r2 = π (10-2π)2 = 10-4 m2.
  2. Resistivity: ρ = RAl = 10 × 10-410 = 10-4 Ω m.
  3. Current density: J = σ E = Eρ = 1010-4 = 105 A/m2, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: A = pi r^2 = 1e-4 m^2, rho = RA/l = 1e-4 ohm m, so J = E/rho = 10/1e-4 = 1e5 A/m^2.

question.stem: Plane angle and solid angle have

solution.full_text:
1. Plane angle $= \frac{\text{Arc}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{[\mathrm{L}]}{[\mathrm{L}]} \longrightarrow$ Unit $=$ Radian
2. $= [\mathrm{M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}}]$
3. Solid angle $= \frac{\text{Area}}{(\text{Radius})^{2}} \longrightarrow$ Unit $=$ Steradian
4. $= \frac{\mathrm{L^{2}}}{\mathrm{L^{2}}} = [\mathrm{M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}}]$
5. $\therefore$ Both have units but no dimensions
solution.html:
1. Plane angle = ArcRadius = [L][L] ⟶ Unit = Radian
  2. = [M0L0T0]
  3. Solid angle = Area(Radius)2 ⟶ Unit = Steradian
  4. = L2L2 = [M0L0T0]
  5. ∴ Both have units but no dimensions
steps: Plane angle $= \frac{\text{Arc}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{[\mathrm{L}]}{[\mathrm{L}]} \longrightarrow$ Unit $=$ Radian
Solid angle $= \frac{\text{Area}}{(\text{Radius})^{2}} \longrightarrow$ Unit $=$ Steradian
$= \frac{\mathrm{L^{2}}}{\mathrm{L^{2}}} = [\mathrm{M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}}]$
$\therefore$ Both have units but no dimensions
printed_lines: ∴ Both have units but no dimensions

steps: Plane angle $\theta = \frac{\text{arc}}{r}$ has dimensions $\frac{[L]}{[L]} = [M^0L^0T^0]$ but unit radian (rad).
Solid angle $\Omega = \frac{A}{r^2}$ has dimensions $\frac{[L^2]}{[L^2]} = [M^0L^0T^0]$ but unit steradian (sr).
So both have units but no dimensions, which is option $1$.

2. For second excited state $\Rightarrow n = 3$

question.full_text:
Two pendulums of length $121\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ start vibrating in phase. At some instant, the two are at their mean position in the same phase. The minimum number of vibrations of the shorter pendulum after which the two are again in phase at the mean position is:
(1) 11
(2) 9
(3) 10
(4) 8
question.html:

  2. (2)9
  3. (3)10
  4. (4)8
question.stem: Two pendulums of length $121\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ start vibrating in phase. At some instant, the two are at their mean position in the same phase. The minimum number of vibrations of the shorter pendulum after which the two are again in phase at the mean position is:

solution.full_text:
1. $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$
2. Let $n_1$ and $n_2$ be integer.
3. $n_1 T_1 = n_2 T_2$
4. $2\pi n_1\sqrt{\frac{1.21}{g}} = 2\pi n_2\sqrt{\frac{1.00}{g}}$
5. $\Rightarrow \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{11}{10}$
6. $\therefore$ After completion of $11^{\mathrm{th}}$ oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.
solution.html:
1. T = 2πLg
  2. Let n1 and n2 be integer.
  3. n1 T1 = n2 T2
  4. 2π n11.21g = 2π n21.00g
  5. ⇒ n2n1 = 1110
  6. ∴ After completion of 11th oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.
steps: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$
Let $n_1$ and $n_2$ be integer.
$2\pi n_1\sqrt{\frac{1.21}{g}} = 2\pi n_2\sqrt{\frac{1.00}{g}}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{11}{10}$
$\therefore$ After completion of $11^{\mathrm{th}}$ oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.
printed_lines: Let n_{1} and n_{2} be integer.
After completion of 11^{th} oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.

steps: For a simple pendulum $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$, so $T \propto \sqrt{l}$.
$\frac{T_{long}}{T_{short}} = \sqrt{\frac{121}{100}} = \frac{11}{10}$.
They are again in phase at the mean position when $n\,T_{short} = m\,T_{long}$ for whole numbers $n, m$.
$n\,T_{short} = m \cdot \frac{11}{10} T_{short} \Rightarrow 10n = 11m$.
The smallest whole-number solution is $n = 11$, $m = 10$, so the shorter pendulum makes $11$ vibrations, which is option $1$.

1. For a simple pendulum T = 2πlg, so T ∝ l.
  2. TlongTshort = 121100 = 1110.
  3. They are again in phase at the mean position when n Tshort = m Tlong for whole numbers n, m.
  4. n Tshort = m · 1110 Tshort ⇒ 10n = 11m.
  5. The smallest whole-number solution is n = 11, m = 10, so the shorter pendulum makes 11 vibrations, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: T is proportional to sqrt(l), so T_long/T_short = 11/10; they are next in phase when n*T_short = m*T_long, smallest n = 11.

steps: From the figure, the top NAND gate takes inputs $A$ and $B$, so its output is $\overline{AB}$.
The bottom NAND gate takes $\bar{A}$ (through the NOT gate) and $B$, so its output is $\overline{\bar{A}B}$.
The AND gate gives $C = \overline{AB}\cdot\overline{\bar{A}B} = (\bar{A}+\bar{B})(A+\bar{B})$.
$(\bar{A}+\bar{B})(A+\bar{B}) = \bar{B} + A\bar{A} = \bar{B}$.
So $C = 1, 0, 1, 0$ for $AB = 00, 01, 10, 11$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From the figure, the top NAND gate takes inputs A and B, so its output is AB.
  2. The bottom NAND gate takes A (through the NOT gate) and B, so its output is AB.
  3. The AND gate gives C = AB·AB = (A+B)(A+B).
  4. (A+B)(A+B) = B + AA = B.
  5. So C = 1, 0, 1, 0 for AB = 00, 01, 10, 11, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: C = (AB)' . (A'B)' which simplifies to B', giving C = 1,0,1,0 for AB = 00,01,10,11.

solution.full_text:
1. For solid wire
2. Inside point
3. $B = \frac{\mu_0 I r^2}{R^2 \times 2\pi r}$
4. $= \frac{\mu_0 I r}{R^2 \times 2\pi}$
5. $B \propto r$
6. Outside point
7. $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
8. $B \propto \frac{1}{r}$
solution.html:
1. For solid wire
  2. Inside point
  3. B = μ0 I r2R2 × 2π r
  4. = μ0 I rR2 × 2π
  5. B ∝ r
  6. Outside point
  7. B = μ0 I2π r
  8. B ∝ 1r
steps: For solid wire
Inside point
$B = \frac{\mu_0 I r^2}{R^2 \times 2\pi r}$
$= \frac{\mu_0 I r}{R^2 \times 2\pi}$
$B \propto r$
Outside point
$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
$B \propto \frac{1}{r}$
For $r < R$, the enclosed current is $I_{enc} = I\frac{r^2}{R^2}$ (uniform current density).
Ampere's law: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I \frac{r^2}{R^2} \Rightarrow B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} \propto r$.
For $r > R$, $I_{enc} = I$, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I \Rightarrow B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \propto \frac{1}{r}$.
Linear increase inside, $\frac{1}{r}$ decrease outside, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For r < R, the enclosed current is Ienc = Ir2R2 (uniform current density).
  2. Ampere's law: B(2π r) = μ0 I r2R2 ⇒ B = μ0 I r2π R2 ∝ r.
  3. For r > R, Ienc = I, so B(2π r) = μ0 I ⇒ B = μ0 I2π r ∝ 1r.
  4. Linear increase inside, 1r decrease outside, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Inside a uniformly carrying wire B = mu0 I r/(2 pi R^2), proportional to r; outside B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), proportional to 1/r.

question.full_text:
Two point charges $-q$ and $+q$ are placed at a distance of $L$, as shown in the figure. The magnitude of electric field intensity at a distance $R (R >> L)$ varies as:
[Figure: Point charges -q and +q separated by distance L]
(1) $\frac{1}{R^{2}}$
(2) $\frac{1}{R^{3}}$
(3) $\frac{1}{R^{4}}$
(4) $\frac{1}{R^{6}}$
question.html:
Two point charges -q and +q are placed at a distance of L, as shown in the figure. The magnitude of electric field intensity at a distance R (R >> L) varies as:
  1. (1)1R2
  2. (2)1R3
  3. (3)1R4
  4. (4)1R6
question.stem: Two point charges $-q$ and $+q$ are placed at a distance of $L$, as shown in the figure. The magnitude of electric field intensity at a distance $R (R >> L)$ varies as:

figures.text: Point charges -q and +q separated by distance L

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Point charges -q and +q separated by distance L

solution.full_text:
1. For $R >> L$, arrangement is an electric dipole
2. $E = \frac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^{3}}$; where $p = qL$
3. $E \propto \frac{1}{R^{3}}$
solution.html:
1. For R >> L, arrangement is an electric dipole
  2. E = 2p4πε0 R3; where p = qL
  3. E ∝ 1R3
steps: For $R >> L$, arrangement is an electric dipole
$E = \frac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^{3}}$; where $p = qL$
$E \propto \frac{1}{R^{3}}$
printed_lines: For R >> L, arrangement is an electric dipole

steps: The charges $-q$ and $+q$ separated by $L$ form an electric dipole with moment $p = qL$.
For $R \gg L$, the dipole field at any point is $E = \frac{kp}{R^{3}}\sqrt{3\cos^{2}\theta + 1}$.
Hence $E \propto \frac{1}{R^{3}}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The charges -q and +q separated by L form an electric dipole with moment p = qL.
  2. For R ≫ L, the dipole field at any point is E = kpR33cos2θ + 1.
  3. Hence E ∝ 1R3, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: The pair -q, +q separated by L is an electric dipole (p = qL); for R >> L the dipole field varies as 1/R^3.

chapter.name: Electrostatics
chapter.why: The answer depends on the far-field electric field of an electric dipole falling off as 1/R^3.

subtopics.name: Electric Field Due to Electric Dipole
subtopics.why: The answer rests on the far field of an electric dipole (charges -q and +q separated by L, with R >> L) falling off as 1/R^3.

step_list: Recognise the -q, +q pair at separation L with R >> L as an electric dipole and recall that a dipole's field falls off as 1/R^3
difficulty.why: A single recall of how a dipole's far field scales with distance; no calculation is needed.

source.note: Stem figure shows charges -q and +q separated by L; figure placed between the two stem sentences. Stray '2π π' fragment at top of crop belongs to previous question and was excluded. Options read from image as stacked fractions (text layer split numerator/denominator rows).

categories.concept: Two equal and opposite charges a short distance apart form a dipole, whose field at $R\gg L$ falls as $1/R^3$ rather than as a point charge's $1/R^2$

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: Coulomb's $E=kq/R^2$ is the relation reached for whenever charges and a distance are printed, and it is applied to the pair as if a single charge sat there, so the inverse-square dependence is carried into a case where the leading term cancels.
trap.who: a student whose stored field law is the point-charge one and who does not treat $+q$ and $-q$ at separation $L$ as a dipole
trap.feels: $1/R^2$ is the dependence every electrostatics field has to begin with, and both charges in the figure are point charges

steps.text: Each charge on its own produces a field falling as $1/R^2$.
So the pair's field also falls as $1/R^2$.
steps.fix: The charges are equal and opposite, so at $R\gg L$ the two $1/R^2$ terms cancel to leading order and what survives is the dipole term, $1/R^3$.

other_options.proof: I worked out which dependences this configuration can supply: one charge alone gives $1/R^2$, the dipole field gives $1/R^3$, and the dipole potential gives $1/R^2$. Expanding two opposite point charges in powers of $L/R$ stops at the dipole term, so $1/R^4$ is the next multipole's field and needs a charge arrangement the figure does not show. No operation on $+q$, $-q$, $L$ and $R$ returns the fourth power.

$1/R^6$ is not produced by any field expression on this page: the available powers are 2 (point charge, and dipole potential) and 3 (dipole field), and squaring the dipole field would give $1/R^6$ only for an energy, not for the field intensity the stem asks about. It completes the exponent spread 2, 3, 4, 6.

categories.reason: This question requires the far-field dependence of a $+q$, $-q$ pair on distance, demonstrated by 'at a distance $R\,(R\gg L)$ varies as' with four options that are only powers of $1/R$.

question.full_text:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
(Assertion (A)) The stretching of a spring is determined by the shear modulus of the material of the spring.
(Reason (R)) A coil spring of copper has more tensile strength than a steel spring of same dimensions.
(1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(3) (A) is true but (R) is false
(4) (A) is false but (R) is true

  2. (Reason (R)) A coil spring of copper has more tensile strength than a steel spring of same dimensions.
  1. (1)Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
  2. (2)Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

question.stem: Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below

statements.label: Assertion (A)
statements.text: The stretching of a spring is determined by the shear modulus of the material of the spring.

statements.label: Reason (R)

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

solution.full_text:
1. It is true that stretching of spring is determined by shear modulus of the spring as when coil spring is stretched neither its length nor its volume changes, there is only change in its shape.
2. Tensile strength of steel is more than that of copper.
3. Hence Assertion is true and reason is false.

  2. Tensile strength of steel is more than that of copper.

steps: When a coil spring is stretched, the wire of the spring is twisted, so its extension is governed by the shear (rigidity) modulus $G$: Assertion (A) is true.
Steel has a larger elastic modulus and tensile strength than copper ($Y_{steel} > Y_{Cu}$), so a copper spring is not stronger than a steel spring of the same dimensions: Reason (R) is false.
(A) true and (R) false corresponds to option $3$.

  2. Steel has a larger elastic modulus and tensile strength than copper (Ysteel > YCu), so a copper spring is not stronger than a steel spring of the same dimensions: Reason (R) is false.
  3. (A) true and (R) false corresponds to option 3.
ai_solution.why: Stretching a coil spring twists the wire, so it is governed by the shear modulus (A true); steel has greater elastic modulus/tensile strength than copper, so R is false.

chapter.name: Mechanical Properties of Solids
chapter.why: The answer turns on spring stretching being governed by the shear modulus and on steel having greater elastic strength than copper, both elastic-moduli facts of mechanical properties of solids.

subtopics.name: Shear Modulus of Rigidity
subtopics.why: The answer hinges on the assertion being true: stretching of a coil spring is governed by the shear modulus (modulus of rigidity) of its material, since the wire twists rather than elongates.

step_list: Judge the Assertion: recall that when a coil spring is stretched the wire itself twists, so the extension is governed by the shear (rigidity) modulus of the material
Judge the Reason: recall that steel has a greater tensile strength than copper, so a copper spring of the same dimensions is not stronger
Combine the two truth values and pick the matching assertion-reason option
difficulty.why: The work is two separate property recalls from mechanical properties of solids, one about which elastic modulus governs a coil spring and one comparing copper and steel, followed by mapping the pair of truth values onto the option format.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The Assertion is counter-intuitive: a candidate who reasons that stretching means Young's modulus will mark it false, and that wrong route lands on a valid option.

source.note: Assertion (A) and Reason (R) moved to statements; stem keeps the intro and closing instruction lines. Negative words are lower-case 'not'/'false' inside the standard A/R option shells. Image matches text layer.

categories.concept: A coil spring stretches by twisting its wire, so the shear modulus sets its stiffness; and steel, not copper, carries the greater tensile strength

trap.label: reversed
trap.route: The Reason prints the copper-steel comparison the wrong way round, and a student who has the Assertion right and sees that a tensile strength cannot explain a shear modulus lands on 'both true, R not the explanation' with only R's direction misjudged
trap.who: a student who knows NCERT's line that a coil spring's stretching is governed by the shear modulus, and who associates copper with soft, easily drawn wire
trap.feels: copper is the metal taught as ductile and drawn into wire, so 'copper has more tensile strength' reads like a property statement, and the two statements plainly concern different moduli so the no-explanation verdict looks safe

steps.text: A coil spring's extension comes from twisting the wire, so the shear modulus determines it: (A) is true.
Tensile strength is a different quantity from shear modulus, so (R) could not explain (A) in any case.
Copper is the ductile, wire-drawing metal, so take (R)'s claim that a copper spring beats a steel spring in tensile strength as true.
steps.fix: Steel's tensile strength is the larger of the two, which is why springs are wound from steel and not copper, so (R) is false and the verdict is '(A) true, (R) false'.

other_options.who: a student who remembers that springs are wound from steel because of its elastic properties and reads (R) as naming that same material property
other_options.feels: (R) is the only statement that mentions a material property of spring wire, so it reads like the reason behind the choice of modulus in (A)

steps.text: The Assertion is the textbook statement about a spring and the shear modulus.
Grant (R) and treat 'more tensile strength' as the material property that fixes which modulus governs the stretching.
steps.fix: Check (R) on its own first: steel outstrips copper in tensile strength, and tensile strength is not the shear modulus the Assertion names.

other_options.who: a student who reads the word 'stretching' as plain elongation and attaches Young's modulus to it
other_options.feels: stretching a spring looks like stretching a wire, and elongation under a pull is the standard Young's-modulus case

steps.text: Stretching means lengthening, so the governing constant must be Young's modulus and the Assertion is false.
steps.fix: In a coil spring the wire is not pulled along its length but twisted, so it is the shear modulus and not Young's modulus that is at work.

steps.text: With (A) dismissed, accept (R) as the surviving true statement.
steps.fix: Steel's tensile strength exceeds copper's, so (R) is false whatever happens to (A).

categories.reason: This question requires checking two printed physics statements against what the chapter states, demonstrated by the options being the four truth-and-explanation verdicts over 'the stretching of a spring is determined by the shear modulus' and 'a coil spring of copper has more tensile strength than a steel spring of same dimensions'. The trap is tagged reversed rather than half_right because the mechanism is the inverted copper-steel comparison printed in the Reason, which is what every wrong verdict depends on granting.
categories.note: The NOT and FALSE recorded in negative_words_seen come from the standard A/R option wording, not from the task.

question.full_text:
A big circular coil of $1000$ turns and average radius $10\,\mathrm{m}$ is rotating about its horizontal diameter at $2\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. If the vertical component of earth’s magnetic field at that place is $2 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ and electrical resistance of the coil is $12.56\,\Omega$, then the maximum induced current in the coil will be
(1) $0.25\,\mathrm{A}$
(2) $1.5\,\mathrm{A}$
(3) $1\,\mathrm{A}$
(4) $2\,\mathrm{A}$
question.html:
A big circular coil of 1000 turns and average radius 10 m is rotating about its horizontal diameter at 2 rad s-1. If the vertical component of earth’s magnetic field at that place is 2 × 10-5 T and electrical resistance of the coil is 12.56 Ω, then the maximum induced current in the coil will be
  1. (1)0.25 A
  2. (2)1.5 A
  3. (3)1 A
  4. (4)2 A
question.stem: A big circular coil of $1000$ turns and average radius $10\,\mathrm{m}$ is rotating about its horizontal diameter at $2\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. If the vertical component of earth’s magnetic field at that place is $2 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ and electrical resistance of the coil is $12.56\,\Omega$, then the maximum induced current in the coil will be

solution.full_text:
1. $\phi_{B} = NBA\cos\omega t$
2. $\varepsilon = \frac{-d\phi_{B}}{dt} = -NBA\omega(-\sin\omega t)$
3. $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$
4. $i_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{max}}}{R} = \frac{NBA\omega}{R}$
5. $= \frac{1000 \times 2 \times 10^{-5} \times \pi(10)^{2} \times 2}{12.56}$
6. $= 1\,\mathrm{A}$
solution.html:
1. φB = NBAcosω t
  2. ε = -dφBdt = -NBAω(-sinω t)
  3. ε = NBAωsinω t
  4. imax = εmaxR = NBAωR
  5. = 1000 × 2 × 10-5 × π(10)2 × 212.56
  6. = 1 A
steps: $\phi_{B} = NBA\cos\omega t$
$\varepsilon = \frac{-d\phi_{B}}{dt} = -NBA\omega(-\sin\omega t)$
$\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$
$i_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{max}}}{R} = \frac{NBA\omega}{R}$
$= \frac{1000 \times 2 \times 10^{-5} \times \pi(10)^{2} \times 2}{12.56}$
$= 1\,\mathrm{A}$
Rotating about a horizontal diameter, the flux through the coil comes from the vertical component $B_V = 2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$.
$A = \pi r^2 = \pi (10)^2 = 100\pi \approx 314\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
$\varepsilon_{max} = N B_V A \omega = 1000 \times 2\times10^{-5} \times 100\pi \times 2 = 4\pi \approx 12.56\,\mathrm{V}$.
$I_{max} = \frac{\varepsilon_{max}}{R} = \frac{12.56}{12.56} = 1\,\mathrm{A}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Rotating about a horizontal diameter, the flux through the coil comes from the vertical component BV = 2×10-5 T.
  2. A = π r2 = π (10)2 = 100π ≈ 314 m2.
  3. εmax = N BV A ω = 1000 × 2×10-5 × 100π × 2 = 4π ≈ 12.56 V.
  4. Imax = εmaxR = 12.5612.56 = 1 A, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Peak emf = NBA*omega = 1000 x 2e-5 x (pi x 100) x 2 = 12.56 V, so I_max = 12.56/12.56 = 1 A.

chapter.name: Electromagnetic Induction
chapter.why: The answer turns on the peak EMF induced in a coil rotating in a magnetic field, e0 = NBAω (Faraday's law), divided by the coil resistance to give I = 1 A.

subtopics.name: AC Generator
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the peak emf of a coil rotating in a magnetic field, e0 = NBAω (here 4π V), divided by the resistance to give 1 A, which is the AC generator relation.

step_list: Compute the coil area A = pi r^2 for r = 10 m
Apply the peak emf of a rotating coil, e_max = N B A omega, using the vertical field component (the field cut by a coil rotating about a horizontal diameter)
Divide by the resistance, I_max = e_max / R, noticing the 12.56 ohm value cancels the factor of 4 pi
difficulty.why: Substituting into the rotating-coil peak emf formula after computing the area, then applying Ohm's law, is a short chain of linked substitutions needing no insight.

categories.concept: A coil rotating in a field has peak emf $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega$, and the peak current is that emf divided by the resistance

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: The flux through the coil swings from $+NBA$ to $-NBA$, and reading that swing of $2NBA$ as the quantity to multiply by $\omega$ doubles the emf to $8\pi$ V and the current to exactly 2 A.
trap.who: a student who derives the emf from the change in flux over a half turn instead of quoting the peak value $NBA\omega$
trap.feels: the factor 2 comes from a true statement about the flux reversing, and the arithmetic then lands on a whole number, 2 A

steps.text: $NBA\omega=1000\times2\times10^{-5}\times\pi(10)^2\times2=4\pi\approx12.57$ V and $R=12.56\,\Omega$.
The flux reverses, so use $2NBA\omega=8\pi$ V, giving $I=8\pi/12.56=2$ A.
steps.fix: The peak emf of a rotating coil is $NBA\omega$, the maximum of $NBA\omega\sin\omega t$; the reversal of flux is already inside that sine.

other_options.proof: 0.25 A needs an emf of $\pi$ V, a quarter of the correct $4\pi$ V, and no printed quantity supplies that quarter. The stem gives a radius, not a diameter, so the area is not divided by four; using the rms value divides by $\sqrt{2}$ and gives 0.71 A; halving $\omega$ gives 0.5 A; dropping the squaring of $r$ gives 0.1 A. None of these is 0.25 A.

1.5 A needs an emf of $6\pi$ V, i.e. the correct value multiplied by 1.5, and nothing in the stem supplies a factor of 1.5 or 3: the numbers combine as $N=1000$, $B=2\times10^{-5}$ T, $A=100\pi$ m$^2$, $\omega=2$ rad s$^{-1}$ and $R=4\pi\,\Omega$, whose only easy variants are the doubling (2 A), the halving (0.5 A) and the quartering (0.25 A). No route reaches 1.5 A.

categories.reason: This question requires $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega$ evaluated and divided by the resistance, demonstrated by 'the maximum induced current in the coil' with $N=1000$, $r=10$ m, $\omega=2$ rad s$^{-1}$, $B=2\times10^{-5}$ T and $R=12.56\,\Omega$.
categories.note: The resistance 12.56 $\Omega$ is $4\pi$ to three figures, which is what makes the answer the round 1 A.

question.full_text:
The volume occupied by the molecules contained in $4.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ water at STP, if the intermolecular forces vanish away is
(1) $5.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$
(2) $5.6 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$
(3) $5.6 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$
(4) $5.6\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$
question.html:
The volume occupied by the molecules contained in 4.5 kg water at STP, if the intermolecular forces vanish away is
  1. (1)5.6 × 106 m3
  2. (2)5.6 × 103 m3
  3. (3)5.6 × 10-3 m3
  4. (4)5.6 m3
question.stem: The volume occupied by the molecules contained in $4.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ water at STP, if the intermolecular forces vanish away is

solution.full_text:
1. From ideal gas equation
2. $PV = nRT$
3. $\left[n = \frac{\text{mass of water}}{\text{mol. wt.}} = \frac{4.5 \times 10^{3}}{18}\right]$
4. $V = \frac{nRT}{P}$
5. At. STP $\Rightarrow T = 273\,\mathrm{K}$
6. $P = 10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/m^{2}}$
7. $V = \frac{4.5 \times 10^{3}}{18} \times \frac{8.3 \times 273}{10^{5}} = 5.66\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$
solution.html:
1. From ideal gas equation
  2. PV = nRT
  3. [n = mass of watermol. wt. = 4.5 × 10318]
  4. V = nRTP
  5. At. STP ⇒ T = 273 K
  6. P = 105 N/m2
  7. V = 4.5 × 10318 × 8.3 × 273105 = 5.66 m3
steps: From ideal gas equation
$PV = nRT$
$\left[n = \frac{\text{mass of water}}{\text{mol. wt.}} = \frac{4.5 \times 10^{3}}{18}\right]$
$V = \frac{nRT}{P}$
At. STP $\Rightarrow T = 273\,\mathrm{K}$
If the intermolecular forces vanish, the molecules behave as an ideal gas, so at STP one mole occupies $22.4\,\mathrm{L}$.
$n = \frac{4500\,\mathrm{g}}{18\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 250\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$V = 250 \times 22.4\,\mathrm{L} = 5600\,\mathrm{L}$.
$5600\,\mathrm{L} = 5600 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^{3}} = 5.6\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. If the intermolecular forces vanish, the molecules behave as an ideal gas, so at STP one mole occupies 22.4 L.
  2. n = 4500 g18 g mol-1 = 250 mol.
  3. V = 250 × 22.4 L = 5600 L.
  4. 5600 L = 5600 × 10-3 m3 = 5.6 m3, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: With no intermolecular forces water behaves as an ideal gas: 4500 g / 18 g/mol = 250 mol, and 250 x 22.4 L = 5600 L = 5.6 m^3.

chapter.name: Thermodynamics
chapter.why: The answer depends on treating the water molecules as an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces) and using the ideal gas molar volume at STP: 250 mol x 22.4 L = 5.6 m^3, which is the 'Ideal Gas Equation' topic listed under Thermodynamics.

subtopics.name: Ideal Gas Equation
subtopics.why: The answer treats the 250 mol of water as an ideal gas at STP, so its volume is 250 x 22.4 L = 5.6 m^3 from the ideal gas molar volume.

step_list: Recognise that vanishing intermolecular forces means treating the water as an ideal gas at STP
Find the number of moles from 4.5 kg of water using molar mass 18 g/mol
Multiply by the molar volume 22.4 L/mol and convert litres to cubic metres
difficulty.why: The work is reading 'forces vanish' as an ideal-gas condition, then doing a mole count and a molar-volume substitution with a litre-to-cubic-metre conversion.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The options differ only by powers of ten, so a slip in the kg-to-g or L-to-m^3 conversion lands exactly on a distractor.

categories.concept: 4.5 kg of water is 250 mol, and at STP each mole of gas occupies 22.4 L, which must then be turned into cubic metres

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: $250\times22.4=5600$ comes out of the mole count and the molar volume, and the figure is then matched to the option carrying 5600 without the litres being converted, so a volume in litres is read as cubic metres.
trap.who: a student who gets the chemistry right -- 4500/18 = 250 mol, 22.4 L each -- and treats the arithmetic as finished at 5600
trap.feels: 5600 is the number the calculation actually produces, and $5.6\times10^3$ is the only option that shows it

steps.text: $4.5$ kg of water is $4500/18=250$ mol, and at STP that is $250\times22.4=5600$ L.
Read 5600 off as the answer: $5.6\times10^3$ m$^3$.
steps.fix: 1 m$^3$ = 1000 L, so 5600 L is 5.6 m$^3$, and the options are in m$^3$.

solution.full_text:
1. Electronic configuration of Gadolinium
2. $\mathrm{Gd}$ :— $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^{7}\,5d^{1}\,6s^{2}$
3. In case of $3^{\mathrm{rd}}$ ionisation enthalpy electron will be removed from $5d$ and resultant configuration will be $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{7}$ that is stable electronic configuration as it will have high exchange energy, hence less energy will be required to remove $3^{\mathrm{rd}}$ electron.

  2. Gd :— [Xe] 4f7 5d1 6s2

steps: Gd ($Z=64$) has configuration $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$.
After two ionisations, $\mathrm{Gd^{2+}} = [\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 5d^1$.
The third ionisation removes the $5d^1$ electron, giving $\mathrm{Gd^{3+}} = [\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7$, a half-filled $4f$ subshell.
The half-filled $4f^7$ state is stabilised by high exchange enthalpy, so $\Delta_i H_3$ is low, which is option $2$.

  2. After two ionisations, Gd2+ = [Xe] 4f7 5d1.
  3. The third ionisation removes the 5d1 electron, giving Gd3+ = [Xe] 4f7, a half-filled 4f subshell.
  4. The half-filled 4f7 state is stabilised by high exchange enthalpy, so Δi H3 is low, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Gd2+ is [Xe]4f7 5d1; losing the 5d electron leaves a half-filled 4f7 configuration stabilised by high exchange enthalpy, so the third ionisation enthalpy is low.

In a Frenkel defect no cation is lost from the crystal, so (R) does not explain why a solid with missing cations is neutral: (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both correct, (R) not the explanation, which is option $2$.

  3. In a Frenkel defect no cation is lost from the crystal, so (R) does not explain why a solid with missing cations is neutral: (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
  4. Both correct, (R) not the explanation, which is option 2.

steps: Benzene with $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ and anhydrous $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ undergoes electrophilic substitution: $\mathrm{C_6H_6 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{FeCl_3} C_6H_5Cl + HCl}$, giving chlorobenzene.
Phenol does not form a diazonium salt with $\mathrm{NaNO_2/HCl}$ (that needs a primary aromatic amine), so option $2$ fails.
Benzene does not react with $\mathrm{HCl}$ alone, so option $3$ fails.
Aniline with $\mathrm{HCl}$ on heating only forms anilinium chloride, not chlorobenzene (no diazotisation), so option $4$ fails.
Hence the suitable sequence is option $1$.

steps: $\mathrm{KO_2}$ is a superoxide containing the $\mathrm{O_2^-}$ ion, so each O has oxidation number $-\tfrac{1}{2}$.
$x + 2\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +1$, so the statement that K is $+4$ is incorrect.

Alkali metals react with water to give $\mathrm{MOH}$ and $\mathrm{H_2}$; ionisation enthalpy decreases down the group; Li has the most negative $E^\circ$ and is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution, so statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct.
The incorrect statement is option $2$.

  2. x + 2(-12) = 0 ⇒ x = +1, so the statement that K is +4 is incorrect.
  3. Alkali metals react with water to give MOH and H2; ionisation enthalpy decreases down the group; Li has the most negative E° and is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution, so statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct.
  4. The incorrect statement is option 2.
ai_solution.why: KO2 is potassium superoxide (O2^-), so K is +1, not +4; the other three statements are correct (Li is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution).

1. Dalton’s law of partial pressure states that the total pressure by the mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of individual gases.
2. $p_{\mathrm{Total}} = p_1 + p_2 + p_3$
3. Also, $p_i = \chi_i p$ ; where $p_i$ and $\chi_i$ are the partial pressure and mole fraction of $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ gas respectively and $p$ is the total pressure.

5. $= n_1\frac{RT}{V} + n_2\frac{RT}{V} + n_3\frac{RT}{V}$
6. $= (n_1 + n_2 + n_3)\frac{RT}{V}$

solution.full_text:
[Figure: I. nitrophenol (benzene ring with OH and an NO₂ group drawn from the ring centre, position not fixed)]
1. Nitro group has electron withdrawing tendency. It can withdraw electrons both by $-I$ effect and $-R$ effect. Thus the acidic strength of monosubstituted nitrophenol is higher than phenol.
2. Nitro group present at o- and p-positions will have strong $-R$ effect while nitro group present at m-position will influence only $-I$ effect hence acidity or o/p isomer will be more meta isomer.

steps: Statement I: $-\mathrm{NO_2}$ is electron-withdrawing ($-I$, and $-R$ at the o/p positions), so it stabilises the phenoxide ion, and every mononitrophenol is more acidic than phenol. Statement I is true.

Statement II: the $-R$ effect works only from the ortho and para positions, and o-nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, so the acidity order is $p > o > m$ ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 7.1, 7.2, 8.3$). The acidities are not the same, so Statement II is false.
I is correct and II is incorrect, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Statement I: -NO2 is electron-withdrawing (-I, and -R at the o/p positions), so it stabilises the phenoxide ion, and every mononitrophenol is more acidic than phenol. Statement I is true.
  2. Statement II: the -R effect works only from the ortho and para positions, and o-nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, so the acidity order is p > o > m (pKa ≈ 7.1, 7.2, 8.3). The acidities are not the same, so Statement II is false.
  3. I is correct and II is incorrect, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: The -NO2 group withdraws electrons, so every nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol (I true); the o-, m- and p-isomers differ in acidity (p > o > m) because the -R effect acts only at o/p and o has intramolecular H-bonding (II false).

(4) $\mathrm{2CuSO_4(aq) + 2Ag(s) \rightarrow 2Cu(s) + Ag_2SO_4(aq)}$

4. Fibres possess high tensile strength.

In one molal solution that contains $0.5$ mole of a solute, there is

solution.full_text:
1. Molality is the moles of solute dissolved per kg of solvent therefore $500\,\mathrm{g}$, $1$ molal solution contains $0.5$ of solute, as
2. $m = \frac{\text{Moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent (in kg)}}$
3. $1 = \frac{0.5}{\text{Mass of solvent (in kg)}}$
4. $\therefore$ Mass of solvent (in kg) $= 0.5$
5. $= 500\,\mathrm{g}$

steps: Molality is defined as $m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{W_{\text{solvent}}\,(\mathrm{kg})}$.
Rearranging, $W_{\text{solvent}} = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m} = \frac{0.5\,\mathrm{mol}}{1\,\mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$.
$0.5\,\mathrm{kg} = 500\,\mathrm{g}$ of solvent, which is option $2$.

  3. 0.5 kg = 500 g of solvent, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Molality = moles of solute / kg of solvent, so 0.5 mol / 1 mol kg^-1 = 0.5 kg = 500 g of solvent.

Given below are half cell reactions:
$\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$,
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/MnO_4^-}} = -1.510\,\mathrm{V}$
$\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2O}$,
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{O_2/H_2O}} = +1.223\,\mathrm{V}$
Will the permanganate ion, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ liberate $\mathrm{O_2}$ from water in the presence of an acid?
(1) Yes, because $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = +0.287\,\mathrm{V}$

Given below are half cell reactions:
MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O,
E°Mn2+/MnO4- = -1.510 V
12O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O,
E°O2/H2O = +1.223 V
Will the permanganate ion, MnO4- liberate O2 from water in the presence of an acid?
  1. (1)Yes, because E°cell = +0.287 V
  2. (2)No, because E°cell = -0.287 V
  3. (3)Yes, because E°cell = +2.733 V

question.stem:
Given below are half cell reactions:
$\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$,
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/MnO_4^-}} = -1.510\,\mathrm{V}$
$\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2O}$,
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{O_2/H_2O}} = +1.223\,\mathrm{V}$
Will the permanganate ion, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ liberate $\mathrm{O_2}$ from water in the presence of an acid?

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \longrightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$ $\quad \ldots(\mathrm{i})$
2. $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}} = -E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/MnO_4^-}} = 1.51\,\mathrm{V}$
3. $\mathrm{H_2O \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2}O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^-}$ $\quad \ldots(\mathrm{ii})$
4. $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{O_2/H_2O}} = 1.223\,\mathrm{V}$
5. Using $2 \times (\mathrm{i}) + 5 \times (\mathrm{ii})$, net cell reactions is
6. $\mathrm{2MnO_4^- + 6H^+ \longrightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + \frac{5}{2}O_2 + 3H_2O}$
7. $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{C}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{A}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{O_2/H_2O}} = 1.51 - 1.223 = 0.287\,\mathrm{V}$
8. Since $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} > 0$, therefore net cell reaction is spontaneous and so $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ liberate $\mathrm{O_2}$ from $\mathrm{H_2O}$ in presence of an acid.
solution.html:

  2. E°MnO4-/Mn2+ = -E°Mn2+/MnO4- = 1.51 V
  3. H2O ⟶ 12O2 + 2H+ + 2e-    …(ii)
  4. E°O2/H2O = 1.223 V
  5. Using 2 × (i) + 5 × (ii), net cell reactions is
  6. 2MnO4- + 6H+ ⟶ 2Mn2+ + 52O2 + 3H2O
  7. E°cell = E°C - E°A = E°MnO4-/Mn2+ - E°O2/H2O = 1.51 - 1.223 = 0.287 V
  8. Since E°cell > 0, therefore net cell reaction is spontaneous and so MnO4- liberate O2 from H2O in presence of an acid.

steps: The given $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/MnO_4^-}} = -1.510\,\mathrm{V}$ is an oxidation potential, so $E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}} = +1.510\,\mathrm{V}$.
Permanganate is reduced (cathode) and water is oxidised to $\mathrm{O_2}$ (anode).
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{anode}} = 1.510 - 1.223 = +0.287\,\mathrm{V}$.
$E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} > 0$, so the reaction is spontaneous: yes, $\mathrm{O_2}$ is liberated, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The given E°Mn2+/MnO4- = -1.510 V is an oxidation potential, so E°MnO4-/Mn2+ = +1.510 V.
  2. Permanganate is reduced (cathode) and water is oxidised to O2 (anode).
  3. E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 1.510 - 1.223 = +0.287 V.
  4. E°cell > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous: yes, O2 is liberated, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: E(Mn2+/MnO4-) = -1.510 V is an oxidation potential, so the reduction potential of MnO4-/Mn2+ is +1.510 V; E_cell = 1.510 - 1.223 = +0.287 V > 0, so MnO4- oxidises water to O2.

chapter.name: Electrochemistry
chapter.why: The answer depends on computing E°cell from the two standard electrode potentials and using its sign to judge feasibility, which is taught under cell potential and standard electrode potential in Electrochemistry.

subtopics.name: Cell Potential
subtopics.why: The answer depends on computing the standard cell potential from the two half-cell potentials (E°cell = 1.510 - 1.223 = +0.287 V) and using its positive sign to judge that the reaction is feasible.

step_list: Read the unconventional Mn2+/MnO4- label as an oxidation potential and convert it to the reduction potential of MnO4-/Mn2+ (+1.510 V)
Assign MnO4- reduction as the cathode and oxidation of water to O2 as the anode, so E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 1.510 - 1.223
Evaluate E°cell (+0.287 V) and use its sign to decide that the reaction is spontaneous
difficulty.why: The work is a sign-convention conversion of one given electrode potential followed by a standard E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode subtraction and a spontaneity check from the sign.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The MnO4- potential is printed as an oxidation potential (Mn2+/MnO4- = -1.510 V); taking it at face value gives -1.510 - 1.223 = -2.733 V (option 4), and mixing conventions gives the +2.733 V and -0.287 V distractors, so each wrong option is the exact result of a plausible sign error.

source.note: Transcribed from image; the electrode potential is printed as E° for Mn2+/MnO4- = -1.510 V exactly as in source (copied as printed, not changed).

Water is written on the left of the oxygen half-cell, so oxygen is the one reduced: $1.223 - 1.510 = -0.287\,\mathrm{V}$, and the answer is No.
steps.fix: Read what the question asks: permanganate is to liberate $\mathrm{O_2}$ from water, so permanganate is reduced and water oxidised, giving $1.510 - 1.223 = +0.287\,\mathrm{V}$.

other_options.who: a student who treats the two printed potentials as contributions to be totalled
other_options.feels: both half-reactions are printed as reductions with a potential each, so adding them reads like combining the two halves of the cell

steps.text: Both half-cells contribute to the cell potential.
So $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}} = 1.510 + 1.223 = +2.733\,\mathrm{V}$.
steps.fix: One half-cell runs in reverse inside the cell, so the two potentials subtract; only one of them changes sign.

other_options.who: a student who takes the stem's $-1.510\,\mathrm{V}$ at face value as the reduction potential of permanganate
other_options.feels: the minus sign is printed in the stem, so carrying it into the subtraction looks like using the given data as given

steps.text: The permanganate half-cell is the one reduced, so its potential goes in first.
That potential is $-1.510\,\mathrm{V}$, so $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}} = -1.510 - 1.223 = -2.733\,\mathrm{V}$ and the answer is No.
steps.fix: The stem writes the couple as $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/MnO_4^-}$, product over reactant, so $-1.510\,\mathrm{V}$ is the oxidation potential and the reduction potential of $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ is $+1.510\,\mathrm{V}$.

question.stem:
What mass of $95\%$ pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ will be required to neutralise $50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.5\,\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{HCl}$ solution according to the following reaction?
$\mathrm{CaCO_{3(s)} + 2HCl_{(aq)} \rightarrow CaCl_{2(aq)} + CO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}}$
[Calculate upto second place of decimal point]

solution.full_text:
1. Let $m$ gram mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ is required
2. Pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in $m$ gram $= \frac{95}{100} \times m$
3. Moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{m}{100}$
4. Moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$ required $= 2 \times$ moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$
5. $= 2 \times \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{m}{100}$
6. $2 \times \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{m}{100} = \frac{50}{1000} \times 0.5$
7. $m = 1.315\,\mathrm{g} \approx 1.32\,\mathrm{g}$
solution.html:
1. Let m gram mass of CaCO3 is required
  2. Pure CaCO3 in m gram = 95100 × m
  3. Moles of CaCO3 = 95100 × m100
  4. Moles of HCl required = 2 × moles of CaCO3
  5. = 2 × 95100 × m100
  6. 2 × 95100 × m100 = 501000 × 0.5
  7. m = 1.315 g ≈ 1.32 g

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}$, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}(\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a}}) = 4.57$
2. $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ \quad $0.01\,\mathrm{M}$
3. $50\,\mathrm{mL}$ \quad $50\,\mathrm{mL}$
4. It is a mixture of weak acid and salt of its conjugate base. Hence it is acidic buffer.
5. $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a}} + \log\frac{[\mathrm{Salt}]}{[\mathrm{Acid}]}$
6. $= 4.57 + \log\left(\frac{0.1}{0.01}\right)$
7. $= 4.57 + 1$
8. $= 5.57$

steps: Sodium acetate with acetic acid forms an acidic buffer, so $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$.
Equal volumes ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$ each) are mixed, so the ratio is $\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = \frac{0.10}{0.01} = 10$.
$\mathrm{pH} = 4.57 + \log 10 = 4.57 + 1 = 5.57$, which is option $1$.

question.full_text:
If radius of second Bohr orbit of the $\mathrm{He^{+}}$ ion is $105.8\,\mathrm{pm}$, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$ ion?
(1) $158.7\,\mathrm{pm}$
(2) $15.87\,\mathrm{pm}$
(3) $1.587\,\mathrm{pm}$
(4) $158.7\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$
question.html:
If radius of second Bohr orbit of the He+ ion is 105.8 pm, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of Li2+ ion?
  1. (1)158.7 pm
  2. (2)15.87 pm
  3. (3)1.587 pm
  4. (4)158.7 ˚A
question.stem: If radius of second Bohr orbit of the $\mathrm{He^{+}}$ ion is $105.8\,\mathrm{pm}$, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$ ion?

solution.html:
1. rn ∝ n2Z
  2. r3(Li2+)r2(He+) = (n3)2Z(Li2+) × Z(He+)(n2)2
  3. r3(Li2+)105.8 = (3)23 × 2(2)2
  4. = 105.8 × 32
  5. r3(Li2+) = 158.7 pm
steps: $r_n \propto \frac{n^2}{Z}$
$\frac{r_3(\mathrm{Li^{2+}})}{r_2(\mathrm{He^{+}})} = \frac{(n_3)^2}{Z(\mathrm{Li^{2+}})} \times \frac{Z(\mathrm{He^{+}})}{(n_2)^2}$
$r_3(\mathrm{Li^{2+}}) = 158.7\,\mathrm{pm}$
Bohr radius: $r_n = a_0 \frac{n^2}{Z}$, so $r \propto \frac{n^2}{Z}$.
$r = 105.8 \times \frac{3}{2} = 158.7\,\mathrm{pm}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Bohr radius: rn = a0 n2Z, so r ∝ n2Z.
  2. For He+, n=2, Z=2: n2Z = 42 = 2, so 2a0 = 105.8 pm.
  3. For Li2+, n=3, Z=3: n2Z = 93 = 3.
  4. r = 105.8 × 32 = 158.7 pm, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Bohr radius r is proportional to n^2/Z: He+ (n=2,Z=2) gives 2 units = 105.8 pm, Li2+ (n=3,Z=3) gives 3 units = 158.7 pm.

question.full_text:
Copper crystallises in fcc unit cell with cell edge length of $3.608 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$. The density of copper is $8.92\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Calculate the atomic mass of copper.
(1) $63.1\,\mathrm{u}$
(2) $31.55\,\mathrm{u}$
(3) $60\,\mathrm{u}$
(4) $65\,\mathrm{u}$
question.html:
Copper crystallises in fcc unit cell with cell edge length of 3.608 × 10-8 cm. The density of copper is 8.92 g cm-3. Calculate the atomic mass of copper.
  1. (1)63.1 u
  2. (2)31.55 u
  3. (3)60 u
  4. (4)65 u
question.stem: Copper crystallises in fcc unit cell with cell edge length of $3.608 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$. The density of copper is $8.92\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Calculate the atomic mass of copper.

solution.html:
1. d = ZMNA(a)3
  2. Z = 4(FCC), d = 8.92 g cm-3, NA = 6.023 × 1023, a = 3.608 × 10-8 cm
  3. M = dNA(a)3Z
  4. = 8.92 × 6.023 × 1023 × (3.608 × 10-8)34
  5. = 8.92 × 6.023 × 1023 × 46.97 × 10-244 = 2523.47 × 10-14
  6. = 630.8 × 10-1 = 63.08 ≃ 63.1 u
steps: $d = \frac{ZM}{N_A(a)^3}$
$M = \frac{dN_A(a)^3}{Z}$
For an fcc unit cell, $Z = 4$ atoms per cell.
Density relation: $d = \frac{Z M}{a^3 N_A}$, so $M = \frac{d\,a^3 N_A}{Z}$.
$M = \frac{252.3}{4} = 63.07 \approx 63.1\,\mathrm{u}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For an fcc unit cell, Z = 4 atoms per cell.
  2. Density relation: d = Z Ma3 NA, so M = d a3 NAZ.
  3. a3 = (3.608 × 10-8 cm)3 = 46.97 × 10-24 cm3.
  4. d a3 = 8.92 × 46.97 × 10-24 = 418.96 × 10-24 g.
  5. d a3 NA = 418.96 × 10-24 × 6.022 × 1023 = 252.3 g mol-1.
  6. M = 252.34 = 63.07 ≈ 63.1 u, which is option 1.

chapter.name: The Solid State
chapter.why: The answer comes from the cubic unit cell density relation d = Z*M/(a^3*N_A) with Z = 4 for fcc, which is solid state.

subtopics.name: Density and Edge Length Calculations for Cubic Unit Cells
subtopics.why: The answer comes from the density formula d = ZM/(a^3 N_A) for an fcc cell (Z = 4), solved for M using the given edge length and density.

step_list: recall that an fcc unit cell contains Z = 4 atoms
cube the edge length to get the cell volume a^3 (about 4.70 x 10^-23 cm^3)
rearrange d = Z M / (a^3 N_A) to M = d a^3 N_A / Z and evaluate
difficulty.why: The work is one recall (Z for fcc) plus a rearrangement of the density formula with a cube-and-multiply calculation involving powers of ten.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: One option is exactly half another, which is the result of using Z = 8 (counting corners as whole atoms) or a wrong Z, so a slip in the atom count lands on a listed option.

source.note: Text layer draft had a trailing stray 'ZM' fragment after the stem; not present in the image, excluded.
